analysis.title: The Commodities Feed: Oil plunges following US midterm elections
key_insights: ICE Brent settled 8.7% lower on 4 November, below $95/bbl, and selling continued in early trading on 5 November. The trigger was the Democrats winning both the House and Senate in the US midterms, which raised hopes of a quicker end to the war with Iran.

ING argues the speed and size of the oil selloff look overdone. Democratic control of Congress means more scrutiny of the war and harder funding, but new members only start in January, which leaves room for Trump to escalate. Trump has suggested there are no imminent plans to strike Iran.

Before the midterms, all signals pointed to Trump resuming strikes. That is less clear now. Without escalation, ING expects oil to keep giving back the risk premium built in recent months, with Persian Gulf oil flows holding up well. An agreement between the US and Iran could remove the premium faster.
ING says oil fundamentals are looking softer, shown by weaker physical markets and timespreads.
EIA data showed US commercial crude inventories fell 865k barrels on the week. Including strategic reserve releases, total crude inventories fell 1.26m barrels.

Distillate fuel oil inventories fell 3.57m barrels even though refinery utilisation rose 1.7 percentage points to 94.5%. Total distillate stocks dropped below 100m barrels for the first time since 2003. Gasoline inventories fell 222k barrels.

TTF European gas fell more than 3.8% on 4 November and kept falling on 5 November, to around EUR85/MWh, on hopes that the midterm outcome speeds a recovery in LNG flows. ING still calls the European gas market fundamentally tight.
EU gas storage is 74% full and has started to draw with the heating season. The end-of-winter position depends on how much Persian Gulf LNG flow recovers, and weather matters more than usual.
Spot gold rose more than 3% on 4 November and moved back above $4,000/oz. ING cites expected legislative gridlock, lower Treasury yields and a weaker dollar as the drivers.
Central banks added 61 tonnes of gold in September per the World Gold Council. Q3 purchases were 228 tonnes (-7% y/y), with Poland and China leading.

ING says the near-term outlook for gold is still challenging. Inflation concerns support expectations of tighter monetary policy, and much depends on Middle East developments and their effect on energy.

sector_views.rationale: Oil is likely to keep giving back its risk premium absent escalation, but ING thinks the latest selloff is overdone given the uncertainty over US policy toward Iran.

macro_indicators.indicator: EIA US commercial crude oil inventories
macro_indicators.interpretation: A small draw. Including strategic reserve releases, the total crude draw was 1.26m barrels.

macro_indicators.reading: -3.57m barrels w/w, total stocks below 100m barrels
macro_indicators.interpretation: Distillate stocks fell despite higher refinery runs, and are at the lowest since 2003. This is supportive for middle distillate prices.
Higher utilisation did not stop distillate stocks from drawing.
Storage has started drawing with the heating season, so the winter outcome depends on Persian Gulf LNG flows and weather.

macro_indicators.reading: 61 tonnes in September, 228 tonnes in Q3 (-7% y/y)
macro_indicators.interpretation: Official-sector demand remains strong, led by Poland and China.

risk_factors: Trump could escalate against Iran before the new Congress is seated in January.
Renewed strikes on Iran would reverse the oil selloff and rebuild the risk premium.
A cold winter combined with little recovery in Persian Gulf LNG flows would tighten the European gas market.
Inflation concerns and expectations of tighter monetary policy could cap gold.
Oil fundamentals are softening, as seen in the physical market and timespreads.
geopolitical: US midterm elections: Democrats won both the House and Senate, which raises hopes for a quicker end to the war with Iran through more scrutiny and harder funding of the war.
New senators and House members start in January, which leaves room for Trump to escalate against Iran in the meantime.
Trump has suggested there are no imminent plans to strike Iran.
The US maritime blockade of Iran is ongoing, and Persian Gulf oil flows are holding up well.
A possible US-Iran agreement could remove the oil risk premium faster.
Persian Gulf LNG flows may recover, and the extent of that recovery drives Europe's gas outlook this winter.

tension_points.bull_case: Oil can rebound if Trump escalates against Iran before the new Congress starts in January. ING calls the selloff overdone, and distillate stocks are the lowest since 2003.
tension_points.bear_case: Democratic control of Congress brings more scrutiny and harder funding of the war. Without escalation oil keeps giving back its risk premium, and a US-Iran agreement would remove it faster. Physical markets and timespreads are weakening.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Renewed US strikes on Iran would invalidate the bear case. A US-Iran agreement would accelerate the premium unwind.

theme_stances.key_argument: Without escalation the oil market is likely to keep giving back the risk premium built in recent months.
theme_stances.evidence: likely to continue to slowly give back the risk premium
